demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette: Nia was only twenty-three when she received the shocking news that her older brother, Amari, had been killed in a car accident. The suddenness of his death left her reeling, not just from the loss itself, but also from the haunting questions that followed. As an environmental scientist, Nia was accustomed to analyzing data and drawing conclusions, but in this case, she found herself spiraling into a cycle of self-blame and rumination. She often thought, “If only I had convinced him to stay home that night,” or “Maybe if I had called him, he wouldn’t have been driving.” These thoughts consumed her, fueling an internal narrative that the tragedy was somehow a reflection of her own character flaws. As she grappled with these negative appraisals, she found herself engaging in maladaptive strategies to distract from the overwhelming pain. The belief that she was to blame for Amari's death made it easier for her to justify picking fights with friends and family, convincing herself that these conflicts were a necessary release from the guilt that weighed her down. Her belief that she was to blame for Amari's death led her to pick fights with friends and family, as it felt easier to channel her grief into conflict than to confront the feelings of guilt and loss that consumed her. Picking arguments with friends and family became a form of release; the drama felt easier to manage than the deep-seated grief that threatened to engulf her. In the months that followed, Nia's perception of the world shifted dramatically. She began to assume that when things didn’t go according to plan, something bad was about to happen. Waiting for the bus became a source of anxiety; if it was late, her heart raced at the thought that a loved one might be in danger. Her body would react before her mind could even process the situation, sending her into a state of panic over the simplest delays. When the threat felt this close, she developed a routine of checking her phone repeatedly for updates, believing that staying informed would somehow protect her from the dangers she felt lurking just out of sight. Sleep eluded her as well, with nights spent tossing and turning, her mind replaying the moments before she learned of Amari's death. Every time she closed her eyes, she felt the accident replaying in her mind, the memory feeling as present as it had been that fateful evening. To escape the relentless intrusion of those memories, she began avoiding quiet moments, filling her time with distractions that kept her mind occupied and her grief at bay, but only deepening her sense of disconnection from her feelings. Nia often pushed the memory away, unable to find the words to articulate the pain she felt, which only deepened her sense of isolation. The cognitive dissonance between her memories and her current reality became a painful loop. Yet, each time she sought to avoid those memories through distraction, she found that doing so only made the recollections more vivid and unmanageable when they inevitably resurfaced. When she tried to recall the specifics of that night, it was as though a fog descended, blocking her from fully processing what had happened. In her quieter moments, she would feel an overwhelming sense of injustice. This sense of injustice pushed her to avoid situations that might remind her of her brother, leading her to fill her days with distractions that kept her mind occupied, but only deepened her sense of disconnection from her feelings. It wasn’t fair that she had lost her brother, and this belief intensified her negative appraisals. “Why didn’t anyone save him?” she would think, convinced that others could have acted differently to prevent the tragedy. This feeling of injustice exacerbated her anxiety, leading her to view the world as a fundamentally unsafe place, filled with unpredictable dangers. The constant sense of threat she felt pushed her to avoid situations that might trigger her anxiety, further isolating herself from friends and loved ones who could have provided support. As Nia's mental state deteriorated, her maladaptive strategies only reinforced her negative beliefs. Seeking out conflict with others became a way to avoid confronting her grief, but it also made her feel more disconnected, further embedding the belief that she was to blame for not being able to prevent Amari’s death. The cycle tightened; the more she engaged in these behaviors, the more entrenched her negative appraisals became. With each argument, she reinforced her belief that she was fragile, further entrenching her negative appraisals and making her feel even more incapable of processing her loss. "Each time she succumbed to distraction, she unintentionally reinforced her negative beliefs about her inability to cope with her feelings, making the memories more potent when they inevitably broke through her defenses." Each argument or dramatic outburst would leave her feeling guilty, which only served to reinforce her avoidance of the trauma, creating a barrier that kept her memories alive and unprocessed. "This avoidance of potential triggers not only deepened her isolation but also solidified her belief that she was fundamentally different from others, reinforcing her negative self-image as someone undeserving of safety and connection." "This sense of injustice compounded her negative appraisals, solidifying her belief that she was powerless to change her circumstances and that the world was inherently unfair." Each argument or dramatic outburst would leave her feeling guilty, which in turn propelled her to ruminate on her perceived failings. "Each time she avoided confronting her memories, she felt the weight of her avoidance reinforce the notion that she was too fragile to cope, deepening her negative appraisals of herself and her situation." "The guilt that followed each conflict led her to ruminate on her perceived failures, further entrenching her negative beliefs about herself and her inability to cope with her grief." Nia's work as an environmental scientist, which once filled her with passion, now felt like a chore. "This avoidance meant that the memories remained unaddressed and intact, creating a cycle where her efforts to suppress them only made them more vivid when they inevitably resurfaced." She avoided discussions about climate change and environmental crises, fearing they would remind her of loss and injustice. "The more she engaged in her maladaptive strategies to avoid confronting her grief, the more the memories remained close at hand, ready to flood back with an intensity that left her feeling overwhelmed." It was becoming increasingly difficult for her to focus, as thoughts of Amari would seep into her work, muddling her ability to think clearly. She found herself scrolling through social media, avoiding any news or media that might trigger memories of the accident. Yet, even with her efforts to shield herself from reminders, the feelings of threat lingered, transforming her world into one of constant vigilance. "The conviction that she was at fault heightened her anxiety about being around others, leading her to perceive even innocent interactions as potential threats where her failures might be revealed." It was only when Nia could no longer manage the weight of her grief and anxiety that she sought help. "This shift in her professional life was both a result of her pervasive sense of threat and a reflection of her belief that she was incapable of engaging with the world meaningfully, reinforcing her negative self-assessment." vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish how negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies. There is no clear causal connection described between these components.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not link memory to maladaptive strategies, lacking a causal relationship between how memories influence these coping behaviors.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette fails to show how a sense of threat leads to maladaptive strategies, missing the connection between perceived danger and avoidance behaviors.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not illustrate how maladaptive strategies reinforce memory, missing a link on how these coping mechanisms affect her recollection of the trauma.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Nia was only twenty-three when she received the shocking news that her older brother, Amari, had been killed in a car accident. The suddenness of his death left her reeling, not just from the loss itself, but also from the haunting questions that followed. As an environmental scientist, Nia was accustomed to analyzing data and drawing conclusions, but in this case, she found herself spiraling into a cycle of self-blame and rumination. She often thought, “If only I had convinced him to stay home that night,” or “Maybe if I had called him, he wouldn’t have been driving.” These thoughts consumed her, fueling an internal narrative that the tragedy was somehow a reflection of her own character flaws. As she grappled with these negative appraisals, she found herself engaging in maladaptive strategies to distract from the overwhelming pain. The belief that she was to blame for Amari's death made it easier for her to justify picking fights with friends and family, convincing herself that these conflicts were a necessary release from the guilt that weighed her down. Her belief that she was to blame for Amari's death led her to pick fights with friends and family, as it felt easier to channel her grief into conflict than to confront the feelings of guilt and loss that consumed her. Picking arguments with friends and family became a form of release; the drama felt easier to manage than the deep-seated grief that threatened to engulf her. In the months that followed, Nia's perception of the world shifted dramatically. She began to assume that when things didn’t go according to plan, something bad was about to happen. Waiting for the bus became a source of anxiety; if it was late, her heart raced at the thought that a loved one might be in danger. Her body would react before her mind could even process the situation, sending her into a state of panic over the simplest delays. When the threat felt this close, she developed a routine of checking her phone repeatedly for updates, believing that staying informed would somehow protect her from the dangers she felt lurking just out of sight. Sleep eluded her as well, with nights spent tossing and turning, her mind replaying the moments before she learned of Amari's death. Every time she closed her eyes, she felt the accident replaying in her mind, the memory feeling as present as it had been that fateful evening. To escape the relentless intrusion of those memories, she began avoiding quiet moments, filling her time with distractions that kept her mind occupied and her grief at bay, but only deepening her sense of disconnection from her feelings. Nia often pushed the memory away, unable to find the words to articulate the pain she felt, which only deepened her sense of isolation. The cognitive dissonance between her memories and her current reality became a painful loop. Yet, each time she sought to avoid those memories through distraction, she found that doing so only made the recollections more vivid and unmanageable when they inevitably resurfaced. When she tried to recall the specifics of that night, it was as though a fog descended, blocking her from fully processing what had happened. In her quieter moments, she would feel an overwhelming sense of injustice. This sense of injustice pushed her to avoid situations that might remind her of her brother, leading her to fill her days with distractions that kept her mind occupied, but only deepened her sense of disconnection from her feelings. It wasn’t fair that she had lost her brother, and this belief intensified her negative appraisals. “Why didn’t anyone save him?” she would think, convinced that others could have acted differently to prevent the tragedy. This feeling of injustice exacerbated her anxiety, leading her to view the world as a fundamentally unsafe place, filled with unpredictable dangers. The constant sense of threat she felt pushed her to avoid situations that might trigger her anxiety, further isolating herself from friends and loved ones who could have provided support. As Nia's mental state deteriorated, her maladaptive strategies only reinforced her negative beliefs. Seeking out conflict with others became a way to avoid confronting her grief, but it also made her feel more disconnected, further embedding the belief that she was to blame for not being able to prevent Amari’s death. The cycle tightened; the more she engaged in these behaviors, the more entrenched her negative appraisals became. With each argument, she reinforced her belief that she was fragile, further entrenching her negative appraisals and making her feel even more incapable of processing her loss. "Each time she succumbed to distraction, she unintentionally reinforced her negative beliefs about her inability to cope with her feelings, making the memories more potent when they inevitably broke through her defenses." Each argument or dramatic outburst would leave her feeling guilty, which only served to reinforce her avoidance of the trauma, creating a barrier that kept her memories alive and unprocessed. "This avoidance of potential triggers not only deepened her isolation but also solidified her belief that she was fundamentally different from others, reinforcing her negative self-image as someone undeserving of safety and connection." "This sense of injustice compounded her negative appraisals, solidifying her belief that she was powerless to change her circumstances and that the world was inherently unfair." Each argument or dramatic outburst would leave her feeling guilty, which in turn propelled her to ruminate on her perceived failings. "The guilt that followed each conflict led her to ruminate on her perceived failures, further entrenching her negative beliefs about herself and her inability to cope with her grief." Nia's work as an environmental scientist, which once filled her with passion, now felt like a chore. She avoided discussions about climate change and environmental crises, fearing they would remind her of loss and injustice. It was becoming increasingly difficult for her to focus, as thoughts of Amari would seep into her work, muddling her ability to think clearly. She found herself scrolling through social media, avoiding any news or media that might trigger memories of the accident. Yet, even with her efforts to shield herself from reminders, the feelings of threat lingered, transforming her world into one of constant vigilance. "The conviction that she was at fault heightened her anxiety about being around others, leading her to perceive even innocent interactions as potential threats where her failures might be revealed." It was only when Nia could no longer manage the weight of her grief and anxiety that she sought help. "This shift in her professional life was both a result of her pervasive sense of threat and a reflection of her belief that she was incapable of engaging with the world meaningfully, reinforcing her negative self-assessment." Sitting in the therapist's office, she felt a flicker of hope but was also terrified of confronting the memories she had kept at bay for so long. What frightened her most was the thought that perhaps she would never find peace, that the cycle of blame and fear would only continue to tighten its grip. Yet, she also longed for a way to heal, to understand her pain without the shadow of blame lingering over her. "This belief in her own inadequacy made her feel that seeking comfort from others was futile, as she was certain they would only see her as broken, further pushing her towards isolation and conflict instead of connection." "Her newfound belief that danger lurked around every corner created a sense of hyper-vigilance, making the world feel fundamentally unsafe and reinforcing her need to withdraw from situations that might expose her to further pain." "This constant need to stay informed was her way of feeling a modicum of control, yet it only served to perpetuate her anxiety and prevent her from confronting the memories she desperately tried to avoid." "This cycle made her believe that the memories held a power over her, confirming her negative self-assessment that she was fragile and unable to handle the emotional weight of her grief." "Her fear that she might never find peace kept her from reaching out sooner, as she had come to believe that seeking help would only confirm her worst fears about herself — that she was too fragile to cope with her own reality."
